*Related Questions on Metaculus:*

* [Will a 100 trillion parameter deep learning model be trained before 2026?](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/3656/will-a-100-trillion-parameter-deep-learning-model-be-trained-before-2026/) (resolved as **Yes**)
* [If GPT-4 is announced before 2025, how many parameters will it have (in billions of parameters)?](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/14327/gpt-4-number-of-parameters/)

---

Parameter count is a key attribute of modern machine learning (ML) systems: it has a strong influence on model performance, and on training costs. [Deepchecks describes](https://deepchecks.com/glossary/model-parameters/) parameters as follows:

>The weights and coefficients that the algorithm extracts from the data are known as model parameters. Model parameters of neural networks consider how the predictor variable influences the target variable.

In other words the model [learns these parameters during training](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/difference-between-model-parameters-vs-hyperparameters/) to fit the input data to the appropriate output.

In recent years the number of parameters used in ML models [has increased rapidly](https://epochai.org/blog/machine-learning-model-sizes-and-the-parameter-gap). But, as discussed in [this writeup](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/midXmMb2Xg37F2Kgn/new-scaling-laws-for-large-language-models) (and also [here](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/6Fpvch8RR29qLEWNH/chinchilla-s-wild-implications)), research by DeepMind published in the spring of 2022, along with a model named [Chinchilla](https://www.deepmind.com/publications/an-empirical-analysis-of-compute-optimal-large-language-model-training), suggested that the importance of dataset size relative to parameter count had been underestimated in previous work.

>On March 29th, DeepMind published a paper, "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models", that shows that essentially everyone -- OpenAI, DeepMind, Microsoft, etc. -- has been training large language models with a deeply suboptimal use of compute.
>
>Following the new scaling laws that they propose for the optimal use of compute, DeepMind trains a new, 70-billion parameter model that outperforms much larger language models, including the 175-billion parameter GPT-3 and DeepMind's own 270-billion parameter "Gopher".

In March of 2022, a paper describing the [BaGuaLu model](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3503221.3508417) model was published, and discussed a variant of this model trained with 174 trillion parameters. However, this was a [sparse model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) (seemingly a variant of [mixture of experts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixture_of_experts)), and was primarily a demonstration of the ability to train large scale models.

Sparse models activate a smaller share of their parameters in a forward pass, using those that were trained for the task at hand, while dense models use a larger share of their parameters. In an ML model a [forward pass](https://ml-cheatsheet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/forwardpropagation.html) or forward propagation is the process of input data "travelling" through the neural network to the output node.

**Predefined Vectors for Memory-Efficient Neural Network Training**
A new methodology called Latent Space Configuration (LSC), proposed by Nikita Gabdullin, an expert at 'Kriptonit', enables neural networks to maintain a fixed model size regardless of the number of classes, solving the scalability issue in machine learning classification tasks. Traditional supervised learning (SL) methods require a classification layer size proportional to the number of classes, making models impractical when dealing with millions of classes—such as in face recognition—due to astronomical memory demands. LSC replaces this approach by projecting inputs (e.g., facial images) into a pre-defined, fixed vector system in abstract latent space. Each class is assigned a unique target vector, and the network learns to map input embeddings as closely as possible to their respective targets while keeping them distant from others. These target vectors are generated using mathematically rigorous constructions like the root system A and its variants, which are uniformly distributed and optimized for separation. This shift from 'one neuron per class' to 'fixed position per class' allows architectures like Vision Transformer (ViT) to remain unchanged even when scaling to 1.28 million classes. In experiments, ViT-S trained with LSC achieved 87.1% accuracy on a 1.28 million-class dataset, demonstrating practical feasibility. Crucially, LSC drastically reduces GPU memory usage: only a small batch of target vectors is loaded per training step, independent of total class count. For example, traditional SL would require a classification layer larger than the backbone model at 100,000 classes, and ViT-B cannot even load a single batch on an A100 40GB GPU with 10 million classes—conditions where LSC remains viable. Additionally, LSC avoids accuracy degradation on known classes when adding new ones, as model parameters remain unchanged. Experiments also show that randomly shuffled vectors (A) outperform uniform distributions in some cases, achieving 87.9% accuracy on ImageNet-1K without data augmentation—comparable to traditional cross-entropy methods but without scalability limitations. LSC is not limited to face recognition and applies to any high-class classification task in computer vision, representing a paradigm shift toward scalable, memory-efficient AI systems.

**Energy-Efficient Deep Learning -- How Precision Scaling Reduces Carbon Footprint | DigitalOcean**
Precision scaling in deep learning reduces the carbon footprint by shifting models from high-precision formats like FP32 to lower-precision representations such as FP16, INT8, and INT4. Fewer bits reduce computational load, memory movement, and power consumption with minimal impact on performance. This method is increasingly adopted for both training and inference. Core concepts include FLOPs (Floating Point Operations per Second), matrix multiplications (MatMuls), tensors, and bits—where fewer bits enable faster compute and lower memory use. Mixed precision training uses FP16 for computation and FP32 for stability, improving speed while maintaining accuracy. Low-precision formats (FP8, INT8, INT4) reduce compute, memory, and energy costs. Quantization stores and computes with lower-bit numbers, especially useful in inference. Key efficiency metrics include throughput (samples processed per second), latency (time per input), GPU hours (compute cost), and memory bandwidth (data movement speed). Training dynamics involve activations, gradients, optimizer states, weights, and KV cache in transformers. Workloads are classified as compute-bound or memory-bound. Additional concepts include epochs, batch size, model size, and the use of PyTorch Lightning and TensorFlow/Keras frameworks to implement mixed precision training efficiently. The article includes practical code examples demonstrating mixed precision, FLOPs, tensors, matrix multiplication, throughput, GPU hours, and quantization in both PyTorch and TensorFlow environments.

**Large language models versus classical machine learning performance in COVID-19 mortality prediction using high-dimensional tabular data - Scientific Reports**
A study published in Scientific Reports evaluates the performance of large language models (LLMs) versus classical machine learning (CML) models in predicting COVID-19 mortality using high-dimensional tabular data from the Tehran COVID-19 cohort, which included 9,134 patients across four tertiary hospitals in Tehran, Iran, from March 2020 to May 2023. The dataset comprised 81 on-admission features, including demographics, comorbidities, vital signs, and laboratory results, with a focus on in-hospital mortality. Data preprocessing included handling missing values via iterative imputation (numerical) and KNN (categorical), normalization using a standard scaler, and feature selection using Lasso regularization, reducing the dataset to 40 top-ranked features. Class imbalance was addressed using SMOTE, increasing the training set from 6,118 to 9,760 samples. For LLMs, data were converted into clinical text narratives, excluding negative symptoms and normal lab values due to context window constraints. Five CML models (logistic regression, SVM, decision tree, KNN, random forest, MLP, XGBoost) were trained with hyperparameter optimization via grid search and cross-validation. LLMs tested included open-source models (Mistral-7b, Mixtral 8×7B, Llama3-8b, Llama3-70b) via Poe, proprietary models (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o) via OpenAI API, and fine-tuned models (BERT, ClinicalBERT). Zero-shot classification was performed without training, while Mistral-7b-Instruct-v0.2 was fine-tuned using QLoRA with 4-bit quantization, mixed-precision training, and gradient accumulation on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and AUC across internal and external validation sets. A 5-fold cross-validation was applied to the training set (n=6,118). SHAP analysis was used to interpret model predictions, with XGBoost serving as the model-agnostic explainer to compute global and individual feature impacts. The study found that CML models outperformed LLMs in predictive accuracy, with XGBoost achieving the highest AUC. However, LLMs demonstrated robust performance in zero-shot settings, particularly GPT-4, though fine-tuning improved results. The influence of training sample size was also analyzed, showing improved performance with larger datasets. The study was conducted under IRB approval (IR.SBMU.RIGLD.REC.004 and IR.SBMU.RIGLD.REC.1399.058), with patient data pseudonymized and protected under the Helsinki Declaration and Iran Ministry of Health regulations. No informed consent was required due to IRB exemption.

The author explains that doubling a layer roughly quadruples the number of weights, causing a rapid increase in computational cost. Every model has a context window that can range from hundreds of thousands to a million tokens. The model’s output is part of the same window as the input.
